instructions: identify the strongest stakeholder against your position and address them
derive one implication your position has for a neighboring policy area, and it must build directly on what instruction 1 produced
identify one piece of missing evidence that would settle the question, and it must build directly on what instruction 2 produced
text:
The practice of tipping in service industries is increasingly viewed as an outdated moral hazard rather than a virtuous custom. I firmly argue that tipping should be abolished immediately to dismantle a system built on economic inequality and arbitrary generosity. While this shift will naturally provoke strong opposition, it is the only path toward genuine workplace fairness.

The strongest stakeholder against abolishing tipping are business owners and managers who benefit from lower overhead costs than they would under a minimum wage model. Their argument rests on financial necessity: if tips were removed, these establishments could not survive without raising base wages or closing their doors entirely. They contend that customers voluntarily choose where to dine based on service quality; therefore, removing the tip lever punishes those who work harder and rewards mediocrity only when a customer feels generous enough to pay extra. This perspective frames tipping as an essential safety net for hospitality workers in low-wage economies. However, this argument ignores the reality that relying on voluntary charity rather than guaranteed compensation creates a volatile environment where employees live paycheck to paycheck based on intangible factors like mood and luck, not skill or effort. The "market choice" is often limited by economic coercion; if one cannot survive without tipping, leaving a low tip effectively means opting out of service entirely due to cost constraints.

This position has a direct implication for neighboring labor policy: the decoupling of restaurant wages from hourly minimum wage standards. Currently, federal law allows employers in the US to pay tipped workers significantly below the standard living wage ($7.25), provided their tips make up the difference. Abolishing tipping forces these businesses to adopt a uniform, livable base wage for all staff regardless of customer whims or location fluctuations. This policy shift would eliminate the two-tiered workforce common in hospitality and align restaurant labor laws with those of other retail sectors. By mandating that service workers earn a full standard minimum wage from day one, the industry could focus resources on efficient scheduling rather than maximizing tip potential to cover basic survival needs. Consequently, this creates a level playing field where compensation is tied strictly to performance and time worked, not customer generosity or geographic arbitrage zones utilized by stingy diners.

To fully settle whether this transition will cause catastrophic business failures as opponents claim, one piece of missing evidence must be identified: comprehensive longitudinal data comparing the financial stability and survival rates of chain restaurants that have voluntarily adopted "service charge" models (where a mandatory 20% fee replaces tips) versus traditional tipping establishments over a five-year period. Currently, we lack concrete metrics on how such transitions affect long-term profitability in high-rent urban areas specifically. Without data showing whether businesses can absorb the increased labor costs while maintaining profit margins and consumer spending habits, proponents cannot confidently predict that abolition will lead to industry-wide collapse rather than just short-term adjustment pains. Gathering this evidence would determine if the "market correction" is a myth or an inevitable necessity for worker dignity.
